title: Mashaw and the limits of procedural balancing
shortTitle: Mashaw and the limits of procedural balancing
summary: Mashaw criticizes an accuracy-centered due-process calculus for overlooking dignity and relying on uncertain measurements of social costs and benefits.
notes:
Jerry Mashaw argues that Mathews narrows procedural value when it treats accuracy as the sole reason for participation. Oral proceedings can confer dignitary benefits, and repeated grant-withdrawal cycles can create demoralization even when later correction supplies money. He also questions treating disability decisions as almost entirely medical and doubting the value of oral explanation. More generally, estimates of the social cost of income transfers and the error-reducing value of hearings may be too uncertain to support a determinate calculation.

The casebook tests doctrinal consistency through Memphis Light, Ingraham, and G & G Fire Sprinklers. It then qualifies its own comparison: West Covina suggests Memphis Light may turn on notice of otherwise inaccessible informal remedies, illustrating how characterization affects a balancing analysis. Brock v. Roadway Express exposes disagreement within a single case about disclosure, confrontation, delay, and whistleblower protection. The notes also discuss Hamdi and Boumediene as difficult settings involving physical liberty and national security. Those are assigned comparative treatments rather than complete opinions.

The concluding point concerns administrative constitutionalism: agencies themselves often decide what procedures a statute’s implementation requires before any court reviews the issue. The source attributes that institutional observation to Adrian Vermeule. It does not imply that judicial review or constitutional minimums cease to apply.
